subtopicTitle: Errors — absolute, relative, percentage; systematic vs random

cards.front: What is the absolute error in a measurement?
cards.back:
The absolute error is the magnitude of the difference between the measured value and the true (or accepted) value of a quantity. It has the same units as the measured quantity.
$$ \text{Absolute Error} = | \text{Measured Value} - \text{True Value} | $$

cards.front: Define relative error and state its formula.
cards.back:
Relative error is the ratio of the absolute error to the true (or accepted) value of the measurement. It is a dimensionless quantity.
$$ \text{Relative Error} = \frac{\text{Absolute Error}}{\text{True Value}} = \frac{| \text{Measured Value} - \text{True Value} |}{\text{True Value}} $$

cards.front: How is percentage error calculated, and what does it represent?
cards.back:
Percentage error is the relative error expressed as a percentage. It indicates the relative size of the error compared to the true value.
$$ \text{Percentage Error} = \text{Relative Error} \times 100\% = \frac{| \text{Measured Value} - \text{True Value} |}{\text{True Value}} \times 100\% $$

cards.front: Distinguish between systematic and random errors in experimental measurements.
cards.back:
• Systematic Errors: Errors that consistently affect measurements in the same direction (always too high or always too low). They are often due to faulty equipment, incorrect calibration, or flawed experimental design. They primarily affect the accuracy of measurements.
  • Random Errors: Errors that cause measurements to vary unpredictably from one reading to the next, sometimes higher, sometimes lower than the true value. They are often due to unpredictable fluctuations in experimental conditions or limitations of reading instruments. They primarily affect the precision of measurements.

cards.front: Provide an example of a systematic error and suggest a method to mitigate it.
cards.back: Example: A thermometer that is consistently miscalibrated and reads $2^{\circ}\text{C}$ higher than the actual temperature. Mitigation: Calibrate the instrument against a known standard, or apply a correction factor to all measurements. For the thermometer, subtract $2^{\circ}\text{C}$ from every reading or re-calibrate it.

cards.front: Provide an example of a random error and suggest a method to mitigate it.
cards.back: Example: Fluctuations in reading a stopwatch due to human reaction time, or minor variations in air currents affecting the measurement of a small mass on a sensitive balance. Mitigation: Take multiple measurements and calculate their average. Random errors tend to cancel out over many trials, leading to a more reliable average value closer to the true value.

cards.front: Why is relative error often more informative than absolute error when comparing the quality of different measurements?
cards.back: Relative error provides context by expressing the error as a fraction or percentage of the measured quantity. An absolute error of $1\text{ cm}$ is highly significant for measuring a $10\text{ cm}$ object (10% relative error) but negligible for measuring a $1\text{ km}$ distance (0.0001% relative error). Relative error allows for a meaningful comparison of measurement quality across vastly different scales, indicating the 'severity' of the error proportionally.

cards.front: If a series of measurements are consistently clustered together but far from the true value, what type of error is dominant?
cards.back: If measurements are consistently clustered together (indicating high precision) but are all significantly offset from the true value (indicating low accuracy), then **systematic error** is dominant. Random errors would cause the measurements to be scattered, even if centered around the true value.
